tagline: Grass holds the dunes in place along a road through ranch country.
intro: Sandhills Journey follows Nebraska Highway 2 for 272 miles between Alliance and Grand Island. The Nebraska Department of Transportation lists it among the state’s scenic byways and records its National Scenic Byway designation. East of Alliance, the highway enters the Sandhills, a region of mixed-grass prairie on dunes held in place by vegetation. Shallow lakes occupy low valleys between dunes, and most of the region has never been plowed. The region sits over the Ogallala Aquifer, whose water reaches the surface in ponds and lakes between the grass-covered dunes.

The towns along this corridor took shape with the railroad. The Chicago, Burlington and Quincy reached Thedford in 1887 and selected Ellsworth for a depot and water stop in 1888. That same year, Bartlett Richards began assembling the Spade Ranch, making Ellsworth its company town. Cattle shipping joined the settlement to the railway. Hyannis was also laid out in 1888 as the railroad reached it.

Drive east from Alliance through Hyannis and Mullen to Thedford. Near Halsey, the Nebraska National Forest interrupts the journey through grassland. At Dunning, Highway 2 turns southeast toward Broken Bow. Continue through Ravenna and Cairo to Grand Island, where the road widens to four divided lanes on the city’s northwest edge.

moments.title: Ellsworth
moments.text: Ellsworth linked a cattle ranch to a railroad: the Chicago, Burlington and Quincy chose it for a depot and water stop in 1888. Bartlett Richards began assembling the Spade Ranch that year and made Ellsworth its company town. Cattle shipped out by rail, while freight wagons carried supplies north to ranch headquarters. A two-story store built in 1898 supplied those wagons. The Old Spade Ranch Store remains the village’s only operating business. The town’s schoolhouse came later, in 1932, and served Ellsworth until 2007, adding a longer civic history to the ranch depot.

moments.title: Nebraska National Forest, Bessey District
moments.text: The Bessey District began as a test of whether forest could be established on treeless Great Plains land. In 1902, botanist Charles Edwin Bessey and Gifford Pinchot persuaded President Theodore Roosevelt to set aside two treeless tracts of Nebraska sandhills as forest reserves. Bessey wanted to grow timber against a feared national shortage caused by fires, unregulated cutting and rising demand for wood. The experiment produced a 20,000-acre planted forest within the larger ranger district. Its Bessey Tree Nursery is listed on the National Register of Historic Places. The ranger district has an office in Halsey.

moments.title: Broken Bow
moments.text: Broken Bow’s name reached the U.S. Post Office Department through homesteader Wilson Hewitt. It likely came from a settler’s discovery of a broken bow in a field at a former Native American camping ground. The town was platted in 1882, before the railroad arrived in 1884. That year it incorporated as a village; city status followed in 1888. Broken Bow is the seat of Custer County.
